title: Consumer Behaviour and Utility: Why We Buy What We Buy

questions.question: In consumer theory, utility refers to:
options: The want-satisfying power of a good, however subjective
The usefulness of a good to society
The money value of a good in the market
The physical durability of a good
questions.rationale: Utility is the expected satisfaction a consumer derives from a good; it is subjective and need not coincide with social usefulness — a harmful product can still have utility to its user.

questions.question: The cardinal approach to utility is associated with:
questions.rationale: Marshall's cardinal approach measured utility in imaginary 'utils'; Hicks and Allen later developed the ordinal approach, which only ranks preferences.

questions.question: When marginal utility is zero, total utility:
options: Starts rising at a faster rate
questions.rationale: TU rises while MU is positive, peaks exactly where MU = 0, and falls once MU turns negative — so MU = 0 marks satiety.

questions.question: Which of the following is a stated assumption of the law of diminishing marginal utility?
options: The good is a rare collectible
Consumption is continuous and tastes are constant
questions.rationale: The law requires homogeneous units, continuous consumption, reasonable size, constant tastes, and rationality; collections and addiction are the standard exceptions.

questions.question: A consumer is in equilibrium (cardinal approach) when:
options: MU of every good is equal regardless of price
Total utility of X equals total utility of Y
questions.rationale: The equi-marginal principle equalises marginal utility per rupee across goods; if MUx/Px > MUy/Py, shifting a rupee from Y to X raises total satisfaction.

questions.question: Two indifference curves can never intersect because:
options: At the crossing point one bundle would yield two different satisfaction levels
The budget line would be violated
questions.rationale: A common point implies the same bundle lies on two curves with different satisfaction levels — a logical contradiction, hence non-intersection is a property of ICs.

questions.question: The slope of a budget line is given by:
questions.rationale: With Px·X + Py·Y = M, the line's slope is Px/Py — the market's rate of exchange; the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) equals this only at the tangency optimum.

questions.question: If a consumer's income rises while prices are unchanged, the budget line:
questions.rationale: Income changes shift the budget line parallel because the slope (Px/Py) depends only on prices; a price change would pivot the line instead.

questions.question: Consumer surplus is defined as:
options: Profit earned by sellers above cost
Total utility minus total expenditure in money terms
What a consumer is willing to pay minus what is actually paid
The rebate given during festival sales
questions.rationale: Marshall's consumer surplus is the excess of willingness to pay over the actual price — the surplus satisfaction enjoyed because price is below maximum valuation.

questions.question: The water–diamond paradox is resolved by noting that price reflects:
questions.rationale: Water has huge total utility but, being abundant, low marginal utility and hence a low price; scarce diamonds have high marginal utility — price tracks marginal, not total, value.
